no. 01 · someone i met once

Griffin

Touch without meaning. They meant it.
red = words Claude changed or added (61%) · tap text to pause autoscroll
PAGE ONE

I met Griffin at a cuddle convention. The premise is that cuddling can be platonic — “touch without meaning.” Reader, I am here to report that a cuddle convention, thrown by a lot of shitty people as a sad excuse for not having a valentine on Valentine’s Day, is not where that happens. Alpha and I had just met and “moved in” together, and we’d decided we weren’t staying home.

Hypothetically, we both wanted to find love. On the bus we made fun of a woman who got on and off with us — then realized she was going exactly where we were going. Outside political-correctness headquarters, Alpha told a stranger the whole consent conversation was bullshit that didn’t need half an hour. We walked in.

She was at the front of the room. Speaking. Behind her, a chalkboard of polite ways to say no. First we practiced rescinding consent. She tried to make it fun by inventing cuddle positions — the alligator, where one person’s legs open like an alligator’s mouth — but the fun was mostly ruined by Alpha sweating at the back.

Then, the second layer of hell: the actual cuddle room, where you discuss, with the people you’re about to cuddle, what saying no feels like. Lucky me, my partner was an organizer. I asked if I could touch her hair. She said, “no, because I don’t think you would be comfortable with that” — then raised her hand and told the whole group she’d said no because she didn’t really think I wanted to touch her hair.

Pointing at me. The creepy one, who’d asked for what they could not have.

PAGE TWO

Then we pretended to be animals. Crawling like hippos. Cuddling like giraffes. Most people were cats or dogs, which I supposed was the point — the platonic cuddle made flesh. I was a sloth. I did not move at all. I waited for it to be over. In the final round I inadvertently found the one attractive male in this sea of potential cuddlers, and perhaps he’d done the same, because we drifted slowly toward each other — a tall boy with a blonde ponytail — along with a woman who told us she was asexual but still liked human contact.

Pillow talk was hopping in our little cuddle threesome, what with him trying to hit on me without hitting on her: we discussed how much we enjoyed that one could cuddle platonically, nothing sexual about it at all, as his hand snaked slowly toward my butt and I moved it gently away. Then the Valentine’s dance, preceded by a barbaric form of slam poetry where the audience stands on their chairs to vote for the poem they liked best.

A great idea, unless your poem tanked and you stared out at a crowd of the seated. I never did like slam poetry, so I stayed in my seat. In the spirit of the convention we held hands the whole way there — myself, the tall blonde boy, a girl with straight hair, and Alpha.

A little hard to pass a four-person cuddle monster on the sidewalk, but, as I always say, “cuddling trumps passerby traffic.” At the dance, Griffin ignored me and flirted with the girl to his left — a petite brunette in glasses and a bright red dress. All evening you could watch his mind turning, working the problem of getting the two of us into bed with him together.

I wasn’t necessarily opposed — not because I was interested in her, but it seemed like an interesting experience to navigate, figuring out what my role would be. She was less interested, and left him for a boy who turned up near the end in a motorcycle helmet, who was, ostensibly, already her partner.

PAGE THREE

Upstairs, over a cider he’d bought, Griffin made a speech about how much power he had, his ability to control people, and how interested I was in having sex with him — then asked me how much I wanted to. I had been thinking no such thing, and told him so, and he backtracked, embarrassed.

He also liked the barbarian lifestyle. In some situations he might act barbaric, or barbarous, if the situation fit. Circumstantially only, he insisted. Normally he was civilized. Then he laid out his plan to bed me and the other girl together, and, for the sake of being unpredictable, I agreed — but first I wandered off to take a call from my brother, who reported he’d seen two salamanders making love in an aquarium that day.

God’s Valentine’s Day gift to the world. Talking to him, my voice changed into the voice of someone familiar, someone with things in common, and I think it put my date off. Downstairs, Griffin asked her whether she wanted to do this. She said no. Then we both danced with other people. Whatever energy there had been had clearly dissipated, but the plan was the plan, so we left together and got on a bus toward his house.

At his street I said I wanted to go home, and he asked if it was because I was afraid he’d force me to do something I wasn’t comfortable with. I said yes. He assured me he would do no such thing, so I agreed, apprehensively. At his house we cuddled on the couch, discussing once more the advantages of cuddling outside a romantic or sexual context.

He carried me to his room. I insisted I no longer wanted to have sex with him. We got naked and did not do anything sexual. In the morning I looked at his extensive Lego collection and he made me eggs, then played a video game while I talked to my friend Alessio. A few months later I ran into him at a party, but I was with another boy, and I didn’t want to talk to him.

no. 02 · someone i met once

Jon

Everything I didn’t say.
red = words Claude changed or added (66%) · tap text to pause autoscroll
PAGE ONE

The first OkCupid date I went on in Portland, I’d spent a whole week messaging men and meeting exactly none of them. Jon Storch broke the streak — mostly because I mentioned I was going to an art museum and he decided that counted as an invitation. I dressed in about four minutes. I looked good, which annoyed me slightly, because I hadn’t tried.

I met him fresh off raw fish and a Sapporo with my friend Alpha, who sized him up, gave him one minute of conversation, and left. Jon looked relieved. He took Alpha’s seat, and when I offered him food and beer he wanted neither and went a little pale — I’m fairly sure he thought I was fattening him up for the check.

Maroon hipster sweater. Tight jeans. Gaunt in the face, skinny everywhere else. He talked. Brown, his administration, the newspaper he wrote for, the president who’d resigned in scandal. Here’s the thing I never told him: I watched that woman resign. In person. At my brother’s graduation. From Brown. I knew exactly who she was, and I sat there and let him explain her to me like a stranger.

I nodded a lot. I faked opinions about liberalism I did not have. Then I paid the check with my debit card, which, for reasons I still can’t defend, I found hilarious.

PAGE TWO

Then came the museum tour of a lifetime, if your life is very boring. The Korean prints did nothing for either of us. But I turned a corner and hit a clay sculpture — a little table of shiny, crowned white people — and something lit up. First thing all day. I leaned against the elevator wall and told myself everything was going to be okay.

I don’t know why I needed to hear it. Apparently I did. Highlight of the date: a strange man at a suit of armor. It was tiny, built for the world’s smallest, angriest warrior, and he just started talking to me, confident and funny, while Jon hovered a few feet back. And I ran a full internal debate: do I signal I’m on a date, or talk to this man more, so my actual date understands I’m not especially invested?

Reader, I kept talking to the armor guy. By the modern wing I came back to life, and by the time we left there was real camaraderie between us, mostly built on agreeing no one should put this much art in one building. But here’s what I actually walked out thinking: it had been weirdly hard to say anything true to him all day.

And I realized, right there on the steps, that I might be better off alone. At least alone I still get to have my own thoughts. He knew the books; I knew the art; neither of us had any idea what to do about it. But I’ll give him this — he was smart. Smarter about school than I’ll ever bother to be.

David

He would only give his height in centimeters.
red = words Claude changed or added (26%) · tap text to pause autoscroll
PAGE ONE

David’s photos were abnormal. They emphasized his creamy complexion. He seemed very young for a man — he was, in fact, two years younger than me — but we’d bantered about cats and dreams, so I agreed to meet him at an all-night coffee house I never went to during the day. When I arrived he’d already ordered.

He was standing as far from the counter as humanly possible, so nobody could confuse him for the one paying. I ordered a chai. We sat at a round table. He talked about studying computer science, and I thought, for some reason, that this could be the one. Then I got annoyed. He wasn’t making conversation.

I was talking fast, asking questions, and he was leaned back in his chair, quiet. I said I shouldn’t finish my chai or I’d get even more hyper. He said I should drink the rest and see how hyper I could get. Which didn’t match the impression I’d been getting, so I gave him a few points.

Then I let him finish it instead. At the bus stop I hugged the pole of the bus sign and swung around it and announced this was the same as paying the fare. He stood upright, checking his phone, nervous the bus wouldn’t come on time. He refused to tell me his height in anything but centimeters — something about the system being flawed — and took this strange hill much further than I would have guessed.

Reader, I still don’t know how tall he is.

PAGE TWO

At his house he told me his roommate had never once brought a date over. So all of this was very surprising to him. They had beef. Both vegetarian — but she’d gone vegan, and was now shaming him for keeping butter in the fridge. I couldn’t imagine how two such polite people had come to harbor such total and complete resentment.

Then we made pasta. He handed me a giant block of cheddar to grate. I grated. When I switched to a second, larger grater that worked better, he became very pissy that I’d used two cheese graters. Two graters to clean. Instead of one. I was starting to see how he might be having difficulty getting along with his roommate.

She came home peppy, with her date. They cuddled on the couch with beers and put on Lost in Translation. Beside the couch was a seat salvaged from a car, lever and all. David sat in the car chair. Said nothing further. Refused the beer — I accepted mine — and when they floated a second movie, he said that they could, but that he didn’t want to, and that he could take me home if I wanted.

In the garage he had a motorcycle. It was at that moment I realized I had to pee, which wouldn’t do for my first time on a motorcycle. He’d forgotten our helmets inside. So, panicked, I squatted in his shed, hoping to finish before he came back — but the thought of him reappearing made me pee-shy.

He came out, handed me a helmet, and we rode home, and it was exhilarating. Then we played chess outside. The backyard sheds wouldn’t open. Eventually we abandoned the game and stood awkwardly in the kitchen, saying goodbye without touching. The next time he picked me up, we drank beer at the park, went back to his and played Nooki and fell asleep holding hands, a cat between us.

I dreamt there was another girl in our bed — Molly, maybe — who looked like his cat.

He said I should drink the rest and see how hyper I could get, which didn’t seem to match the impression I was getting so I gave him a few points for that. I gave it to him and he had the rest. I had gone on so many dates that somewhere near the 10 minute mark I felt I had already made too good of an impression, they were ready to marry me, and I knew I would never see them again. Such was not exactly the case, though I can’t say I would have spotted him in a crowd, he was very curious and very stubborn.

When we got to the bus stop, I used one hand to swing freely around the pole and he refused to tell me his height in anything other than centimeters, saying something about the system being flawed. However, he took this very strange hill he’d decided to die on much further than I would have guessed. Needless to say, I still don’t know how tall he is (and perhaps I shouldn’t have asked in the first place). We went to the bus stop. I sat down and hugged the pole of the sign for the bus and said that it was the same as paying the fare and he stayed upright and looked for the bus and checked his phone and told me when it was supposed to come and seemed nervous that it wouldn’t come on time. We got on. I didn’t have a dollar so he gave me enough to finish paying the fair.

We walked to his house. He had told me about a guy he’d seen with a car full of cats, sitting in his driveway with all the cats for a few hours. He pointed out the house. We got to his house.

He told me his roommate had never once since he’d lived there brought a date over, so this was very surprising to him. He seemed to have some beef with his roommate; something to do with they were both vegetarian but she had recently become vegan and was now shaming him for putting things like butter in the fridge. I couldn’t imagine how two such seemingly polite people might have come to harbor such total and complete resentment. But I supposed I’d seen it happen with best of friends.

We sat at the table, not talking very much and then decided to prepare some pasta for dinner together. He had a giant block of cheddar cheese, which he instructed me to grate which I did so, first using a handheld grate, and then I found another larger grater that worked a bit better. At this point he became very pissy that I’d used two different cheese graters when I should only have used one. Two cheese graters to clean, instead of one. I was starting to see how he might be having difficulty getting along with his roommate.

His roommate came home and she was very peppy. We asked each other basic questions about where we were from etc. and I wondered once again how David had possibly gotten on the wrong foot with her. While we ate our two bowls of pasta at the little wooden table, her date came and they cuddled on the couch and drank beer. They invited us both to sit on the couch with them and watch the movie they were planning to watch which was Lost in Translation.

Next to the couch it seems they had salvaged an old seat from a car, which still had the lever to make it lean back. David sat on the car chair and didn’t say anything else after that  and refused the other beer that they offered which I accepted. When they suggested we watch another movie he said that they could but that he didn’t want to and that he could take me home if I wanted.

We went outside and went to his garage where he had a motorcycle. It was at that moment that I realized I had to pee. That wouldn’t do for my first time riding a motorcycle. He had forgotten our helmets inside. Panicked, I squatted, hoping I could somehow pee in his shed before he came back but the thought that he would reappear at any moment made me pee shy. He came out and he gave me a helmet and we got on the back and we rode home and it was exhilarating.

He came in and we decided to play a board game and that we were going to play chess and take it outside. We went outside to explore and we tried to go into the sheds that are in the backyard but we couldn’t open them. Eventually we decided not to play the game and we stood awkwardly in the kitchen saying goodbye without touching.

LATER ENTRY

He picked me up from my house and we drank beer at the park, then went to his house and played Nooki and fell asleep holding hands with a cat between us. I dreamt that there was another girl in our bed (maybe Molly) who looked like his cat. He went to school in the morning and when he got back we had tea in the kitchen and then we went to Los Gorditos and shared a quesadilla and then we got the ladder so he could go onto his roof and plugged stuff in and cut part of the tree down. Afterwards we watched the dream movie with his roommate and then he took me to 51 Licks and drove me home.

I saw the most attractive person I had ever encountered through the window of the Southeast Grind, ten o’clock at night, having a cigarette. I decided he was passing through and I would never speak to him. Reader, he sat three seats away. He was drawing in a sketchbook. One by one the people between us left, until it was just him and me — so I did the natural thing and sprawled across all three empty stools, stomach on the middle one, and asked to see his art.

He showed me. A washed-out watercolor nature scene. Immediately turned off. But I was already there, splayed across three seats. He asked if I wanted to play chess. Of course. He got the board from the games closet and set it up in an interested silence — never asked whether I knew how to play, never asked whether I was any good, which flattered me.

A few moves in, I got bored. So I started to act out. I moved my pawn three spaces instead of two. He said nothing. Took his turn. I took mine. I moved a knight into a cluster of his pieces. Then I moved his pieces. Then two of my own at once. I returned dead pieces to the board.

Finally I killed my king with my own queen and moved it off the board, so that no one could win — and we kept playing anyway, until he had about ten pieces left and I had one white pawn darting around all of them, whether it was my turn or not. “You win,” I said.

He agreed, and set up the board again. I won the second game. Through all of it he stayed stony-faced and unperturbed, following the rules without comment.

PAGE TWO

Outside, I leaned on him, his dark sweatshirt against mine, the cigarette in his hand. He sat down and had me sit on his lap. A friend came over and asked how he was. “Can’t complain,” Jake said. “I got a hot babe on my lap and a hot cigarette on my lips.” He pulled at the lining of my dress.

“Is this a… scarf?” It was not. He leaned in to kiss my mouth, and I turned my head the other way, so that we would not be intimate. Then I turned back around and put my arms around his neck and my legs around his stomach. “You’re a little koala, aren’t you?” he said, in something like disbelief.

He was an artist, he said; the Grind was the only place open all night, and he liked to work on his art there. At the studio he made noodles in a silver cylinder with a pouring spout, in what I could not imagine were clean pans, and handed me the aux cord. PAGE ONE

Blake set our first date in the middle of a forest. A specific fallen tree, on a trail in downtown Portland, reached by directions he’d made obscure on purpose. This, I supposed, was exactly the quirky premise I’d been hoping for, which is, of course, why I agreed. I did not set an alarm, even though I was due to meet him at ten.

Google Maps was dead on my phone, so my roommate plotted the route on his computer, and then I got on the bus and rode it to the completely wrong end of town. In my defense, the sun was slanting through the windows. I got wrapped up wondering what all the other passengers might be doing on this strange day.

People with lives, I supposed. I didn’t have one. It reminded me of days I’d been excused from school with a doctor’s note and left to lounge on the sunny couches in my parents’ bedroom, the light hitting them from an unfamiliar angle, reality shifted a fraction of an inch into an alternate reality where things, vaguely, weren’t as they often were.

I stared at the spot on the map that was supposed to be my hiking trail, saw only concrete, and decided I must be crazy to think that somewhere past all these streets I’d find an all-consuming wilderness. So I stayed seated. When I realized my mistake, I panicked. Waves of caution I hadn’t felt since I awaited a teacher’s realization that I had not, as instructed, written six pages.

A wake-up call. Why were there exactly zero moments of this kind of terror in my daily life? I couldn’t remember the last time I’d felt this alive, and though it wasn’t pleasant, I resolved to do more things. The vaguest of plans. I texted him that I was lost. He said he was enjoying what he was doing in his tree, and that it would still be there when I got there.

A lot of points for him. The rest of the directions: past three fallen trees, across two wooden bridges, and I’d find him. I hadn’t reached a single marker. I went back. I texted him. I went forward. I sat down on the trail and, though my battery was low, listened to Blue by Animal Collective, to collect myself.

Two women confirmed there were, in fact, wooden bridges a little farther up. I walked the way I’d been going all along, got confused again, and called him.

Then he told me he’d written his ex-girlfriend’s senior thesis for her, because she was Asian and couldn’t write English that well.

Reader, this was the seven. There was a couch, a mirror, his arm around me, and we might have kissed. I said I was really tired and just wanted a nap. This was true. At my house I lay down on my bed. He came in, seemed uncomfortable, said this wasn’t what he’d been expecting, said he wanted to cuddle.

Louis

Caturday.

PAGE ONE

Louis was so very cute in all of his pictures that I couldn’t believe he’d want to meet me. He said it was “Caturday” — the day for cats. In person he was cute too, and very lovely, and within ninety seconds he’d claimed my roommate’s giant yoga ball and was bouncing on it. I took the rolly chair.

He’d started doing yoga. He liked dancing. This was going well. We went to Buffalo Exchange on Hawthorne, where he tried on leggings — but first we tried on hats together — and then, while he waited in the chair beside me, I applied for a job. I filled out the whole application. Someone came over and interviewed me on the spot.

This was a date. It was raining and we couldn’t find the car. We found a Mexican restaurant with almost a tiki theme, vegetation climbing to the ceiling, and I panicked about which cocktail to order, not being a person who orders cocktails, so we each got something different and shared. He told me about his last relationship.

Five years. Ended by small things. Then he apologized for talking so long. No, I said. It was interesting. Keep going. So he told me about his next adventure, in which he would go pick weed leaves and then take ayahuasca. He drove me home to change my pants and then took me to a club called Bossa Nova: three probably elderly gentlemen playing live, disco lights in the floor, booths where people drank extravagant cocktails and maybe smoked cigars.

We landed smack in the middle of the dance floor. It was very hot. We were dancing together and he had yet to so much as grab my wrist. This went on for a long while as I contemplated what might possibly be going on. It seemed an obvious time for physical contact. Reader, he did not take it.

Until I said fuck it, broke the rules, and leaned my hand casually on his hip. Two more drinks each, and we were making out in a booth. He drove us back through the rain. We made out in the car. His fingers traveled southward. He asked if I wanted to go inside. Inside, we almost went further, but he asked if I wanted to, and I said no, so we didn’t.

He rolled over and slept completely separate from me. Fell asleep fast. I watched his slow breathing. He left fairly early the next morning.

no. 07 · someone i met once

Patrick

Like a tiger. Or a man proving a point.
red = words Claude changed or added (29%) · tap text to pause autoscroll
PAGE ONE

Patrick came pre-assembled. I met him on the street, beer already in hand, fresh from the 7-Eleven. Lumberjack plaid flannel. Horn-rimmed frames the size of dinner plates. A messy bun perched on a silky mane of light ginger. A carefully constructed hipster, built from the outside in. Me: black tight dress, black skeleton long-sleeve, black Harley-Davidson boots.

Same as yesterday. Same as the ten days before that. Nothing else I own is clean. On the way we passed Michael — gray cardigan, the one t-shirt, holes generous enough to show part of his bare chest shining translucent in the moonlight. He joined us. For more beer, obviously. I went in and bought a very dark porter in a handsome glass bottle.

Not a single beer. A 40. Much too much for me to drink by myself, but I was feeling ambitious. Outside, I found the two of them amiably comparing notes on what they hate about America. Feverish. Hands going. The word capitalism every few seconds, like a hiccup. Both wanted out as soon as possible — China, maybe, or India, where things are cheaper and more community-oriented and there isn’t so much capitalism.

Reader, I could not bring myself to join. I stared instead at the bumps in the paved lot, at the white poles holding up the canopy, at the dark night behind all of it. The more the merrier, you’d think. But no: my date and my friend had claimed each other entirely, leaving none for yours truly.

Then a stranger pulled up in a beat-up van. While his car filled with gas, he approached me — only me — to ask if I had a cigarette. Gauges. Nose piercing. Khaki shorts. I was, frankly, pleased to finally have a companion of my own. Patrick said he’d give him one for fifty cents.

The stranger dug fifty cents from his pocket. Cigarette acquired, he went right back to ignoring my two companions, looked straight at me, and asked, quite aggressively, who these boys were. I answered frankly: I’m on a date with one, the other is my friend. He glanced at Patrick just long enough to gesture at him, and asked whether I felt safe with my date.

PAGE TWO

“Look, you can’t just, like, insult my date like that or whatever, ok. He’s, like, a person and all.” I was mostly hoping the confrontation might buy me a night without the word capitalism. Michael said nothing, did nothing, a shit-eating grin plastered across his face. Patrick stalked closer. Closer. Until he was centimeters from the stranger’s head, staring with his magnificent dark eyes.

Like a tiger. Or a man trying to prove a point. “If we were to fight — just saying — you’d be dead. On the ground in one second.” Then he wrapped his arm lightly around the stranger’s back: “You guys look gay. Oh look, I think they’re gay — don’t you think they might be, like, maybe just a little bit gay, or something?

No? I think they might be.” Michael and I stared at each other across the circle, a hint of mirth on our lips and confusion in our eyes, as our two new friends squared up to fight each other over nothing. So I made an offer. “Do you, like, really wanna hit something, or what?

Cause, you can just hit me.” He didn’t believe me at first. “It’ll be fine, I think. No, seriously.” We went back and forth until he delivered a light slap to the side of my face — not so light as I was expecting. After that, there was nothing to do but leave, so Patrick and I made our way home.

The stranger, presumably, returned to his van; Michael, from the corner of my eye, seated himself at a nearby picnic table. Tension successfully diffused. To what end, exactly, I can’t be sure. At home I fulfilled my promise of letting him sleep in my bed — except he wasn’t ready to sleep. I simply wanted to.

Patrick lay awake beside me, pleading that I hadn’t gotten a chance to know him, that I’d prejudged him, that I’d made a mistake. In the morning he smoked out of a pipe he’d brought and left the ashes on our communal table, where my roommate — this is a substance-free household — saw them before I could.

He texted me later, thanking me for the show. I can only suppose how his account might differ from mine. Still, I think he’d be the main character, since I can’t think of anything out of the ordinary that I said or did.

After this, I can think of nothing to do but leave, and so Patrick and I make our way quickly back home, while chubby stranger most likely returns to his car, and from the corner of my eye, I can make out that Michael has now seated himself at a nearby picnic table. Tension successfully diffused. To what end, exactly, I can’t be sure.

Now Patrick and I are walking home. He comes in, and I fulfill my promise of letting him sleep in my bed. Except he isn’t ready to go to sleep. All thoughts of that strange depressing day having left my mind, I now simply want to sleep. But Patrick lies awake next to me, pleading that I haven’t gotten a chance to get to know him, that I’ve prejudged him, that I’ve made a mistake.

In the morning, he smokes out of a pipe he brought, and leaves the ashes out on our communal table as marijuana smoke fills the air. I, still in bed, ask him to dispose of this waste but when he finally leaves through the side door, I find it still there, but not before my roommate of this substance free household, sees it.

He texts me later, thanking me for the show. I can only suppose how his account might differ slightly from mine. A strange sentiment and I reflect on the events as I suppose he intends, as though they are the plot of a movie. Still, I think he would be the main character, as I can’t think of anything out of the ordinary that I’ve said or done that night previously, or this morning.

no. 08 · someone i met once

Trevor

He smashed a beer bottle over his own head.
red = words Claude changed or added (35%) · tap text to pause autoscroll
PAGE ONE

Trevor called before the date to ask if any of my ex-boyfriends might be out to get him. Someone had just phoned to threaten him — don’t go out with his girl. I said I didn’t know who that could be, and I was fairly sure it wasn’t about me. He didn’t buy it. He was already a little angry, somehow, at me, for a crime I hadn’t gotten around to committing.

He showed up twenty minutes later anyway and ordered a coffee with four shots. Very cute, not very big, a bit like Drake from Drake and Josh. Skinny jeans, black t-shirt. We drove to The Florida Room and took the outdoor patio, where he bought us tequila shots and we read our poetry to each other.

He knew the bartender. The bartender always poured him extra-full shots. This is how I came to be very drunk, drifting over to other people’s tables to talk with them and then inform them they were boring, until Trevor escorted me out. His house was two blocks away. Top floor. I made a lot of noise in the bathroom.

On the stairs up to his attic room, the light caught something on his face — scratches. I asked about them. I only know that because he told me the next day; by then the night had gaps in it. His ex-girlfriend had done something to upset him, he said, so he’d smashed a beer bottle over his own head, to try to kill himself.

A strange story to lead with on a first date. He offered it like it was nothing. In the morning he handed me the remote and said I could put on any movie I wanted, so I put on Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas. The sun came in sweet and yellow. The colors were so pastel and opaque that I decided it was my favorite movie.

As it went on, I liked it less. There was, I realized, sort of no plot. On his ceiling was an electrical outlet, and when he plugged his phone into it, the phone dangled there in the air, pretty far down, turning slowly on its cord. Reader, I watched the phone instead of the movie.

PAGE TWO

He had therapy that afternoon, so he’d have to drop me off after breakfast. We ate big breakfasts. In traffic on the bridge he called his therapist to say he’d be late; his therapist, he told me, really liked him, and wouldn’t mind. By the time we arrived the appointment had already passed, so he called back and — since it was all the way across town — apologized, and cancelled.

We went back to his place and watched television instead. He told me about Mount St. Helens, how a man had caught the eruption in a photograph and sold it to the newspapers for a fortune, and I was amazed, so we went to the computer and he showed me the pictures. He told me about his ex-girlfriend as we walked.

They’d been homeless together for a while, and it had made them very close; now that he had a place to live, she treated him like shit. Never let him talk to other girls. Broke up with him to go out with other boys, then called to say mean things. He’d been meaning to break up with her, he said.

They kept getting back together. We set out for a strip club across the bridge, but he got too tired, so we turned around. He played Venus in Furs on his iPhone — that thin little speaker our only company — and we both knew the words, so we sang along. Later a friend texted about a night club.

The floor was white with lights underneath it, like that game with the polar bears, don’t break the ice, and girls danced on poles, climbing down to mingle. A guy came up to chat me up — Palestinian, I think — and kept telling me I was too cute to bomb. I declined his offer of a drink.

Trevor and I sat out on the curb while he smoked, watching a couple change clothes, or have sex, in a jeep across the street, while a man passed us leading a group of others and swinging a crowbar. Back inside, I danced on the little stage; when a guy on Molly tried to hug me, Trevor gave him a double high five.

And then, when we finally got into bed, his ex-girlfriend called. Something she said made it clear: she had been the threatening call before our date, her voice run through some kind of editing software, disguised. Now she was laughing at him, saying my date had probably gone badly. He said he was still on it.

She got extremely pissed, told him never to call her again, and called back ten times. He didn’t answer. He cried a little. I had a job interview at eleven, and instead I lay awake in the dark, his anxiety coming off him like heat, becoming mine — a kind I hadn’t felt in a while.

It bothered me that he could be so obsessed with this other girl while we were lying in the same bed. I cuddled him at first. Then I stopped. In the morning he drove me to my interview and waited in the car, napping. We had a long kiss before I got out. We made rough plans to see each other again.

I never did find out which of us the threat had really been about.

We heard my roommate enter and he was worried that he would be mad at him. We left the house and I chose music and we discovered that we both loved the kinks and the talking heads. Your notes on Trevor

no. 09 · someone i met once

Gabriel

A policy of not looking at anyone I find attractive.
red = words Claude changed or added (23%) · tap text to pause autoscroll
PAGE ONE

Six sentences into OkCupid, Gabriel asked if I wanted to hang out. By the seventh we had a plan: overalls, Hot Topic, ironic. Then, on the day of, he announced he’d been “just kidding” about the overalls. He’d rather do a park. Reader, I did not like that. So I told him to meet me at my house.

He said I could be a murderer, or a rapist, and that he’d rather meet somewhere public. Not entirely unreasonable — in another mood I might have admired the disregard for gender norms — but I reconsidered whether I wanted to meet him at all, and cancelled our date right then and there. He seemed surprised.

So I changed my mind. The outfit mattered now. I went into my room to make sure I was wearing something that didn’t scream “I don’t care if you think I’m pretty”: a white ruffly button-down I’d never once considered wearing, which I thought perfect for my current sentiments. Roll-on deodorant. And, since I was going all out, I combed my hair with my fingers and got engrossed in how much I could change its state.

Then, since I had to wait for his call, I fell backwards onto my bed and lay there half-dreaming about absolutely nothing — and missed his call by seven minutes. He didn’t pick up when I called back. So I texted him pictures of food and animals and smileys blowing heart kisses, walked the three houses to our meeting spot, and settled down next to a yield sign to study the percentage of white flowers embedded in the grass.

I hadn’t been outside yet that day. The gentle sun mushed my shoulders forward, sweetly. He finally called from a few streets away, coming from work painting houses. His boss had criticized his work and cited it as the reason for his less-than-ideal pay, to which he’d replied: “then it’s great that you’re paying me what you are.”

I suggested this might have been a less than strategic response. Then I asked if we could meet for only a very short time, so we wouldn’t have to suffer through an entire date — and caught myself. This reluctance, this uneasiness, was exactly the quality I hated most in my own dates. So I left it at an invitation to my little intersection of white-flowered grass, and told him to see me not as a date but as a friend to be funny with.

He came into view riding his bike like a steed — sitting fully upright, hands cradling the phone.

PAGE TWO

I told him I liked his pants, and that was the last I saw of him, as I have a policy of not looking at anyone I find attractive. The policy had come into effect, for the first time, that day. “Are you smoking a cigarette?” I asked. I wouldn’t have to ask, he pointed out, if I’d been looking at him — which was one hundred percent the case — and I fell down laughing on the grass, imagining having to explain the policy’s reasoning to him.

His pants, it turned out, were spattered with paint from his job. He was disappointed, he said, that people always commented on them. They were just his work clothes. He didn’t think they were cool. What I ideally would have noticed was the gold chain underneath the rim of his t-shirt. I noted that I did not have x-ray vision.

This elaborate reasoning escaped him. So I told him I would start looking at him, and that I was weird, and after convincing myself everything was the way it always was, I shifted my head in his direction for a second while he talked. I was very proud of myself. His ex-girlfriend, he told me, had become a stripper because she wanted her life to be more “real.”

He seemed to find this silly, so I was, of course, compelled to tell him I was an “aspiring alcoholic” for a surprisingly similar reason. He said everyone in the park was on an OkCupid date, and pointed at a couple in front of us who weren’t wearing much. That was the way to do it, he said.

We should have come in our bathing suits. He was mostly looking to make friends in Portland, since all his childhood friends had become gangster drug-addicts. I said I had no friends either, having only recently moved. We decided on beers from a store. While he went inside he told me to watch his bike.

Then, that I should not walk off with it. I was surprised, and could think of no reason he would distrust me. I felt, suddenly, profoundly misunderstood. There was nothing I could do. He came back with a paper bag and we drifted to another park — first the ground, then a picnic table — where he told me he liked to dress up sometimes.

As a goth. In white tracksuits. As a gangster. I told him I didn’t know many boys who liked to play dress-up. I told him what had happened with David, went to show him a picture, and found that I had been unmatched.

PAGE THREE

I chugged the last third of my beer and stood up feeling unhealthily drunk — the air gone opaque, a darker, deeper blue — and assigned myself the task of being extra careful about what came out of my mouth. He didn’t want to pay for my dinner, he said. Then, trying to explain himself, that he didn’t want to pay for his own dinner either.

At Los Gorditos I ordered a chimichanga much too large to finish, and we ate mostly in silence. After the meal he announced that he’d eaten too much and felt sick. Where others might have hidden this, he was straightforward, as though it should be my problem too. How could one ask for support so casually?

I told him he could come sit on my couch for a moment to feel better. At home, I pulled every piece of clothing out of my closet and introduced him to them one by one. His favorite was a bright orange long sleeve with a hologram of a dinosaur. He asked what I’d be doing if he weren’t there.

Honestly? Probably OkCupid. So he made me go on it while he watched. I’d been messaging someone about reading poetry to each other; Gabriel said I should just write “let’s have sex,” so I did. The responses arrived over the next few hours. First, that he lived in North Portland and wanted foreplay. Then, “Oh I get it.

Oh haha like ‘we do sex now.’” Then a third, something about poetry again. Then he saw my drawings and paintings and said, strangely: “Oh, I could actually use you for something — I really need to learn how to paint and draw. You could teach me.” It is and has been my dream to give art lessons to a willing pupil, so I feigned disinterest, then thought better of it and told him I was seriously interested.

When it got late, he said if he was going to bike home he’d better go. Outside, in the dark, standing behind his bike, he was just a glowy outline of a person — white, not much height, but some sort of presence — looking so forlorn. I’d stayed on the porch, under the light, leaving him no opportunity to hug or kiss me goodnight, which is perhaps what I intended.

I said he could sleep on the couch if he really didn’t want to bike. He said he would feel degraded to sleep on the couch. “Do you still want to do art lessons soon?” I asked, and he said, “Oh yeah — can I just, like, start coming by if I’m in the neighborhood?”

I asked if he was being sarcastic, since that seemed a strange thing to ask at the end of a first date. He biked off. Then called twenty-five minutes later: he’d forgotten his backpack. He came back for it, and this time I gave him a hug goodnight.

He’d been 15 at the time and had just run away from home and a girl who went to college had brought him home to her dorm room and he’d been too drunk and high to consider the situation or consent. I told him the story about losing my own virginity.

He told me that it was late and that if he was planning to bike back to his house he had better get going right then. I asked him how far the ride was and if he felt safe biking at night and things like that without saying anything about the possibility of him staying over but without saying particularly that he should leave either.

We went outside together and he got his bike and he was standing behind it on the path that leads to the steps that lead to the front door. It was dark and I couldn’t see all of him, just a glowy outline of a person, a white one with not much height but nevertheless some sort of presence. He looked so forlorn where he was standing behind his bike and I was still standing on the porch, under the light I suppose, and I hadn’t gone down with him when he went to get it and it left him without the opportunity to either hug or kiss me goodnight which is what I perhaps intended. I asked him once again if he felt safe biking so late and he said he did and I said “Alright, see you later.” And he said “Alright see you later.” and I said that if he really didn’t want to bike right then, that he could sleep on the couch and he said he would feel degraded to sleep on the couch.

I said “Oh, do you still want to do like art lessons soon?” and he said “Oh yeah, can I just like start coming by if I’m in the neighborhood?” And I asked if he was being sarcastic cause that seemed like a strange thing to ask at the end of a first date. He said he just wanted to know and I said “Um, yeah, sure, I guess you can come by…” It felt strange to be on the receiving end of hearing something quite so crazy. In truth, I wouldn’t have minded, but didn’t want to say yes in case it were a test about how I would react. And he went to the front door and went to the bathroom first I think and I gave him some water.

He called me about twenty five minutes after he left and said he’d forgotten his backpack at my house and could he come back and get it. I said he could of course and he came back and got it and this time I gave him a hug goodnight.

I slept on the couch that night, with the light on at first, and with my blanket being the sweatshirt that I’d been wearing, the one that Devin had given me but not for keeps but I’d taken it home. I left on videos of Russell Brand and then a variety of other British actors and famous people being interviewed on an English talk show. I woke up at around four in the morning and my sleep had been weird, and I turned off the talk show that kept switching to new episodes on youtube. I went back to sleep still on the couch and woke up refreshed in the morning when my roommate Greg came home from wherever he was. I was still tired and managed to go back to sleep even though it felt like maybe I’d already woken up for good.

THE DRAWINGS

no. 10 · someone i met once

Michael

I’d known him for months. His profile picture was blurry.
red = words Claude changed or added (44%) · tap text to pause autoscroll
PAGE ONE

I had known Michael in person for months before I realized I was also talking to him on OkCupid. We had matched. His profile picture was blurry, and I never put the two together — the man from the cafe and the man on my phone were, as far as I knew, two different men.

They were one man. We met at the Southeast Grind. Repeatedly. None of it turned into hanging out anywhere else, or exchanging numbers, or making plans. The first time, he kept most of his eye contact on his phone — scrolling, clicking, glancing up at me every so often while still, somehow, dominating the conversation, which was about which college major makes the most money.

I stayed in it because it was ridiculous, and I was waiting for my opening to point out how rude he was being. Then he put the phone down. And the conversation got interesting. And I lost my nerve. After that we didn’t greet each other as friends. More as patrons of the same establishment, passing the time.

He did sit next to me, if we came in at once. One night he was already there with a boy named Matt, an activist. I liked Matt for his passion and then, quickly, for nothing, because he was unreasonably idealistic. The three of us went to the all-night pancake house, so it wasn’t really a date.

There we met a homeless man named Jason. I invited him to our table too, not yet knowing how batshit he was. He proposed. He asked me to marry him, and before I could answer he was pulling the pink glass ring off his own finger to give to me. It stuck. He kept pulling.

By the time it came free his finger was bleeding — so now there was blood on the table, and a ring, and a proposal, and I asked for a bandaid because I felt guilty, like maybe I wasn’t supposed to have been talking to him at all. By the end it was just Michael and me, making jokes about Jason.

His method for closing out a night, I learned, was agree-and-then-ignore: oh yeah, it’s getting very late, we should probably go home, a laugh, and then a new topic, until I leaned back against the wall of the booth and fell asleep for a moment. Somewhere in there we invented niplr, a dating site where people meet based solely on pictures of each other’s nipples.

He also wanted an app where you pay for your food in line, which I found much too practical, and I wasn’t sure he understood the game we were playing anymore. Reader, my therapist drove past the cafe, saw us in the window, knew exactly what he was looking at, and whisked me away. You should just date that guy, he said, once he had me.

I think he felt guilty for taking me.

PAGE TWO

Then, on OkCupid — where this whole time I had also been talking to him — we kept up an inane conversation of nonsense until he invited me to a makerspace that happened to be two blocks from where I was standing. I got there. He was deep in conversation with a girl about which colleges they’d gone to.

I joined by standing next to them, unacknowledged, until Michael waved a hand at me and announced that I’d also gone to college in Boston. I’d gone to college in Connecticut. Still — I was mildly impressed he’d remembered anything at all. He went off to make himself a name tag and came back as lobster bisque.

I wasn’t sure this was funny, but told myself perhaps I just didn’t understand the joke. Mine said Sophie. I told the girl that wasn’t even my real name, that I’d been Sage, and she told me I was a coward for changing it to something more normal. That wasn’t the reason I’d given. I liked hers better, so I pretended to identify with it.

I had two separate panic attacks about which beer to drink. Poured one out behind the station. Was still undecided when Michael wandered over, hesitantly, and I bridged the gap between us. I told him a story I probably shouldn’t have, about the night before. He said no, the story was very good, and that we should tell all the people at the party.

We looked around. We didn’t want to tell any of them. So we decided to write a comic book instead. We founded niplr properly — he made a folder for it on his computer, right there — while the girl he’d been talking to wandered the party alone, drifting close sometimes to stare, and I kept saying we should include her and then going back on it, because I didn’t actually want to.

A boy’s ping-pong ball rolled over to me. I picked it up and refused to give it back, so he had to come to me to retrieve it. When the party wrapped, Michael smuggled his beer cup out against his waist, and we walked to his apartment, a longer walk than I anticipated, possibly because I was by then quite drunk, having eaten almost nothing all day except a handful of sample macaroni and cheese I took from New Seasons with my hands on the way through, leaving by the back entrance.

Somewhere in there I hurled my packet of memes into the dog cage I had once been in, myself. At his place I was too drunk for anything but the sofa, and then the porch, where a woman passing by — moving out of her apartment, it looked like — gave me two packets of ramen, because I asked her for food.

She and Michael had a conversation over my head. I don’t know what it was about. I wasn’t paying attention.

Date with Michael Kirschbaum

The thin morning light was already emerging over the trees and it looked as though it were going to be a gray day. no. 11 · someone i met once

Pratfaller

Thick pancakes in the morning, then he asked me to leave.
red = words Claude changed or added (0%) · tap text to pause autoscroll
PAGE ONE

He let me sleep in his bed with him but I refused to let him kiss me He made me thick pancakes in the morning He asked me to leave so he could get ready for work He was playing a rap song called “animal” that I liked We tried riding home on his bike with me on his back He offered to pay for a taxi for me He said he was a very good car salesman and worked so much that he needed to use OkCupid He switched my drink order to non-alcoholic He paid for everything, including the drinks I’d had before he came He shared a room with a girl he was not dating As dictated by our weekly Vision Action Group Meetings, I had an all day meeting with my friend Joey.

When the meeting seemed to be dragging I asked if it would make sense if I left him with some alone time. He didn’t mind my being there, he said, before locking himself in the bathroom for half an hour and coming out to tell me some alone time was what was called for. I left with the unnecessary awkwardness of the situation lingering in the pit of my stomach.

Instead of going home I had a drink at a sushi restaurant on Alberta. After I’d been sitting at the bar by myself for about a half an hour I thought of a potential solution. I fired up the ol’ dating app and started inviting people to meet me. I invited three people and two responded and one came and his name I don’t remember.

I’d been sitting in the same swivel stool for an hour and a half by myself, wondering why my life was so boring and what the difference between being alive and dead really was in this moment when suddenly this lanky blonde man came in, nonchalantly taking a seat next to me. He ordered a drink and struck up a conversation as though we had no meeting planned.

After I’d been sitting at the bar myself I started asking people to meet me. I asked three people and two of them responded and one came and his name I don’t remember (it was jake, I think) but his username was pratfaller. I’d been sitting there for an hour and a half by myself and suddenly this lanky tall blonde-haired guy came in, acting nonchalant as though he didn’t know me and took a seat next to me at the bar and started talking to the bartender and ordering a drink.

I suppose his plan was to tell people we just started chatting at this bar, and never mention the existence of our online communication. But we got chatting and he told me he was a very good car salesman and that the only reason he was on okcupid is because he worked so often that he didn’t have time to meet people.

Strange I had never felt the need to excuse my online dating profile (my life’s blood, the precious gem of my existence). He worked sixty hours a week. He’d lived in Portland all his life he liked biking he made a lot of money he didn’t like his job that much but he was good at it.

I was a little gone; I’d already had two drinks and he bought me a third and himself a third too. I got up to go to the bathroom and remember the revelation of walking down the hall without the pressure of my meeting people costume and trying to have a realization about something about life and nothing was coming to me.

When we got up to leave, he paid for not just the drinks he’d ordered with me but the drinks I’d had before he came with his plastic money machine and signed a white little paper. He took me to a bar down the street and we sat at the counter on two black bar stools.

He seemed to know the waitress there and talked to her for a minute while I went on my phone or something and then he ordered a different drink than I asked him to order: one without alcohol. It took me a little longer than it should have to figure out what he’d done and then I was disappointed because I wanted to get a little more intoxicated I was slipping off my bar stool and messing around with my purse backpack and left to go sit at the fire pit.

I sat there and thought about being unhappy. He came to sit next to me and I was feeling warm and sleepy and not like pretending anything anymore. I have no idea what we talked about; if anything I think he revealed that my new drink didn’t have alcohol. He said his apartment was a 20 minute walk and that I could come if I wanted to.

So I suppose I said yes because next thing I knew we were out in the cold night again, traveling for what seemed like forever to a place I’d never been before that I could not imagine actually existing I wasn’t wearing pants; instead I was wearing a skirt. I kept asking him how much longer the walk was going to be and he kept saying like 20 minutes.

He had his bike and he said he’d have a cab called for me if I wanted and that we could see each other again but I was stubborn and we continued the journey. He offered to have me ride on his back as he biked. It was extremely hard to get on and I wobbled off almost as soon a we started moving.

He said we should try again but it wasn’t a good experience and he wasn’t being nice to me so I said no we could just walk the rest of the way. It took a lot longer. I was drunk and said whatever came into my head. I wasn’t walking very straight either; I remember my limbs were falling all over each other sort of and I felt sort of like a frat bro.

I felt like a very clumsy girl. I couldn’t tell if he liked me at all. I didn’t like him too much then either, since he kept saying slightly mean things to me about my being drunk my not having a job. His building was unexpectedly tall, sleek, and shiny. There was even a lobby with brown carpet and marbled tiles.

And to my surprise, we weren’t even the only one’s arriving here this late; in fact about 5 other people took the elevator alongside us. I was excited to be inside. I didn’t look at him and he didn’t look at me. It was a really silent and calm experience after that strange walk and I felt nothing like I’d felt outside in this warm refuge.

When we got into his little apartment I was surprised to find that he had a female roommate, who’d apparently agreed to sleep on the couch due to my presence. She was small, and maybe Asian, and had all her bed things settled there; a brown duvet, and a fluffy white pillow. I talked to her for a bit before dropping all my things onto the floor in his bedroom where we slept on his twin, perhaps cuddling but I refused to let him kiss me.

I don’t know why. I simply didn’t want it to happen. In the morning he was already awake, tossing some pancakes which we ate at his high table. I remember he had a little speaker over which he played an upbeat rap song which I liked, and I asked him for the artist. I do not know what the mood was that morning; I was very grateful to him for making me pancakes, especially after not letting him kiss me.

I don’t think either of us knew if we’d ever see each other again as we boarded the elevator so that he could be on his way to work.

Sean

The least successful Tinder date of all.
red = words Claude changed or added (0%) · tap text to pause autoscroll
PAGE ONE

This was perhaps the least successful tinder date of all and actually ended in something like a fight. After spending the night at Jake’s house, I was relatively stranded in a part of town that I did not recognize. I figured this was as a good a time as any to get to know new parts of the city, and found myself in a sports bar with a balcony overlooking giant tvs.

Instead of a bar, they had picnic tables dispersed scattered throughout and I spent most of the day here. I talked to a friend on the phone as I wandered upstairs though that part was roped off and thought dejectedly about my constant, nagging loneliness. How could it be this hard to find people to shoot the shit with, besides my friend’s back home?

I left and made plans to meet Sean Niesson on the corner of Everett and 18th….it was kind of a strange place to wait, and I felt rather self-conscious as cars whizzed past me, probably wondering what I was doing standing in the middle of nowhere. It was then, of course, after I’d finally secured plans, that my roommate Alpha asked if I wanted to meet him at The Economics of Happiness Conference which was downtown.

I said I would meet him and go out for dinner with him and a group of friends he’d met at the conference. Sean picked me up on the street corner of Everett and 19th. I remember because I waited in that corner for quite a while, unsure if I’d be waiting there forever. I got into the car and he was immediately unfriendly.

I don’t remember what we talked about. When I got in the car, he did not smile, and barely looked up. Rather than friendly banter, his hands were glued to the steering wheel, his eyes fixed on the road. I have to say I pride myself on being somewhat of an expert at drawing even the stubbornest introvert into casual conversation, but this time it was really like pulling teeth.

The only thing I remember from this conversation is him being surprised that I had a friend, one friend, who lived in Portland, having lived there for three months. He told me he still hung out with his friend from high school, which didn’t sound too bad to be honest. The conference took place in a large hall, that felt a bit like a church I’d been to once.

The seating was stadium style, and the seats were beige, and cushioned. I can understand, in retrospect, that I might not have been the ideal date, at least from his perspective. While he paid rapt attention to the goings on below, I surreptitiously looked at my phone, which had me quite addicted at this point in my life.

It was the last day of a three day conference, and there was a ceremony wherein everyone was invited to get up and dance. At this point, we switched roles to some extent as he faded shyly into the background, and I joined the lively procession from the hall to the lobby. Outside, we settled on a nearby bar, the cheerful tortoise which I’d never been to before, and as we walked the five blocks over the cobbled stones of downtown Portland, I was somewhat surprised to hear that he’d taken in the message, not to mention on board with its way of seeing the world.

Though I hadn’t, perhaps, been paying full attention, I’d managed to take in enough to know I had my doubts, and tried, a bit unsuccessfully, to explain my skepticism. Oh, what was I doing anyway, casting aspersions on what seemed to be an inspiring experience for the young lad? At the bar, I asked for a dinner menu.

This is when our date, which hadn’t been going particularly well up until this point, sort of imploded. It would seem that he was under the impression that I was trying to get him to buy me dinner. Having had nothing but those thick pancakes early that morning, and having finally arrived at an establishment meant for eating, my mind was occupied with nothing but my sudden realization of hunger.

He paid for our beers, and we left, but as we walked back into the street, we sort of stopped interacting, and he left without so much as a “bye.” I was now out on the streets of Portland by myself and it was getting dark. What’s more, my phone wasn’t charged. However, I managed to find an outlet hidden at the base of a telephone pole and just in the nick of time too, as I’d forgotten I’d apparently scheduled another date that was supposed to starting imminently.

In fact, unbeknownst to me, a man had driven from nearby Beaverton, and was sitting, now, in his car, waiting to meet me.

This was perhaps the least successful tinder date of all and actually ended in something like a fight.

no. 13 · someone i met once

Matt

One tiny blurry picture of him playing a red guitar.
red = words Claude changed or added (0%) · tap text to pause autoscroll
PAGE ONE

Matt’s had only one picture on his profile and it was tiny and blurry and depicted him playing a red guitar. However, our conversation on okcupid had entered the realm of absurdity and I was excited to meet someone who’d been conversing with me exclusively about chickens for a day or two. He appeared above my perch by the telephone pole, where I was huddled, still trying to charge my phone.

He wasn’t quite as skinny as those few pixels had made him seem, and he was wearing a gray sweatshirt. He told me his plan was to go to Ground Kontrol, a bar that doubles as an arcade. But at this point, I was all but starving so I redirected us to the nearest restaurant which was a sophisticated Italian place with counter service and only about 5 dishes on the menu.

We split a plate of pasta and a beer and, after my previous date, we split the tab as well. Afterwards we did go to Ground Kontrol. When I asked him if he’d had much luck on okcupid, he told me a story about the other girl he’d met on okcupid who he didn’t like.

Apparently she texted him that she had been waiting in her car for a while and had gotten very sweaty. I started talking to this guy at the booth next to us who was from Colorado. Then my date and I left. He offered to drive me home. I was a little bit drunk and I discovered I’d forgotten to close my tab so he drove me back to Ground Kontrol and I recovered my debit card.

In the car outside my house he gave me a tiny kiss on the lips before I got out. I went inside and saw that he had texted me that he was sorry if he’d “forced the kiss on me.” I didn’t respond I felt awkward as he hadn’t particularly forced me to kiss him, though I can’t say I wanted it to happen either.

Unsure of how to respond, I didn’t. And later, I found out he’d deleted his okcupid after that, apparently so embarrassed about this ambiguous interaction that he’d wanted his online presence to disappear. A few months later, I sent him the invitation for writing a synopsis of how our date went. He didn’t write one but called me one night while I was having dinner with my roommates.

I took the call in the bathroom. He told me that he hadn’t been on any other okcupid dates after ours and that he thought okcupid was home to the kind of girls he didn’t like. It seemed like he meant basic bitches. He said that he’d been confused because he’d thought our date had gone really well but after it was over he reconsidered why he thought that and couldn’t come up with any reasons.

He said that I’d seemed very nervous throughout the date and thought I must have been nervous to be on a date with him but considered that I might somehow be fucking with him and just pretending to be nervous. He said he didn’t know why he’d had us go to Ground Kontrol and that it was because he had planned it and so it was set in his mind.

I was enjoying our conversation and laughing a lot. He told me a story about his roommate peeing on his living room rug that I found hard to believe. I told him I might hang out with him as friends in a few weeks after I became not so busy.

PAGE ONE

In most of his pictures he looked normal — skinny, with pale skin, my type. In one picture, it appeared he had a pointed chin, like a witch. I wondered — was this the most accurate representation of what he actually looked like in real life? I messaged him for a while, I asked him first for a drum lesson and he countered with: coffee or tea? he asked if I thought that was too forward and he interpreted my “yes” as “yes that was too forward.”

I exchanged a phone number with him, but still had surprising difficulty agreeing on a where and when to meet, even after conversing verbally multiple times. Finally, I led him to my favorite spot, due mostly to convenience (the Southeast Grind) for a coffee or tea or something, though it was already really late at night.

I got there before him, I ordered a chai tea that I did not want but felt obligated to consume anyways, I got a call from him, he arrived on his bicycle; I did not see him when I went outside to look and became concerned that I’d given him directions to the wrong place.

Then I saw him, he had the thing I’d thought his face might look like in his profile, sort of like a witches, with a pointy chin and I thought he was also attractive, more so than my last date at least. He was wearing a sleek black “biking’ jacket and I think shorts, which I suppose did not become him (his personality).

We hugged. He didn’t order anything in the cafe, he wanted to go to subway, there was some awkward confusion with me trying to make up a reason why I would also want to go to Subway but it turned out he didn’t care one way or the other. He seemed not incredibly mindful of what I might be thinking at any given moment.

We went to subway. In the line, we talked about our parents, and their jobs. After we walked the few blocks to his drum studio (about 10), and we made forced and very awkward conversation in the small carpeted space that he was renting. I was beginning to feel rather nonplussed by this experience when he showed me what he could do with drumsticks.

In spite of myself, I was impressed, though less so that he seemed to know and think it was impressive himself, too. We sat across from each other at the makeshift table in amidst various stands and paraphernalia, awkwardly perusing each other’s music libraries, noting intermittently when we recognized or liked a song in common.

It wasn’t going very well; and for a moment I felt I’d been transported back to middle school — unable to carry on a full conversation with the opposite gender, reduced to blushes and quick glances of eye contact. I don’t think I knew what he was thinking. I felt for sure he could have ended the date at any time had he not been into me so I assumed shyness.

We plodded on, and finally we had had enough and agreed it was time to go. But first I asked to use the bathroom and he showed me the way. He noted offhandedly that it was cold and I offered him my coat. Veering from his script, he suggested that we switch outfits altogether, and so we did.

He tried on the black evening gown I’d purchased for \$6.99 from Goodwill earlier that day, and I put on whatever he was wearing. There was something incredibly comical about the large protrusion that appeared suddenly in the front, lower half of the dress, bunching the silken material, rippling outward. Back in the little room he was renting, I picked up one of the wooden sticks that littered the floor and used it to find the indentation of his belly button, then penetrated it rhythmically.

After we spent a bit more time in the studio, he walked me home and slept in my bed. Robin

Four a.m. was mid-day to me.

PAGE ONE

Due to my strange sleep schedule, 4am had become a normal time for me to be awake — about the equivalent of mid day — and I didn’t think twice about inviting someone over in the middle of the night. However, when he came over toting a six pack of cider, the implication hit me hard and I scooted slightly away from him, not liking his goofy demeanor.

I sat down cross legged on the porch, thinking it would be warmer in my bedroom but not exactly anxious to invite him inside, considering the uncomfortable situation I found myself in. What’s more my bedroom wasn’t big enough for much more than a bed so that’s where we’d have to hang out. I was wearing a skirt that pulled up a little when I sat down but I remembered it was too dark to catch much of a glimpse.

He sat a little too close to me and I moved back a little and the decision not to hook up with him was made explicit, at least in my mind. He opened our ciders. I drank my first five sips in like one minute. We went back into my room and I set up my little plastic horses and cows on a book and then took the bowling pin from my little toy bowling set and used it to knock them down.

We got into bed and he tried to cuddle with me but I was already facing the other way and didn’t let him touch me and at one point he tried to kiss me. I was feeling tired as I fell asleep I think. In the morning he was there and he told me that he’d gotten a boner in the night and hadn’t known what to do since I’d been asleep.

I wanted to say “fat lot me being awake would’ve done” but instead left his foolish thought to hang in the air. I pulled out two eggs from the refrigerator and turned up the heat on the skillet. I cracked the eggs and they all broke. I left them on too long and they got burned on the bottom and then I didn’t flip them over.

I put bread in the toaster and put the egg on it. The eggs had little pieces of black burnt charcoal on them. I asked my roommate whose lettuce was in the fridge and he said that I could use it so I sprinkled some on the burnt eggs. He said they were the worst eggs he’d ever seen.

I decided never to make breakfast for anyone that came over because it never worked and I didn’t even want to. We each ate a few bites and went back into the other room. He laid in my bed for a while. He told me about a date he’d been on the day before in which he’d driven his friend Sarah somewhere and that they’d had a date in the car.

I told him he shouldn’t be giving people rides for no reason and he said he always did it and it was no big deal. He said that he’d been on the hockey in high school and that he and his co captain had had a thing and that he’d never really gotten over her.

He said they’d been pretty good friends before their feelings were talked about but that they weren’t good friends anymore and that he thought about her all the time and wished that he could be with her. He offered to give me a ride to my friend Amicia’s house and I accepted and then Amicia canceled.

He asked me if I would ever hook up with him and I told him never.

Everyone at once, starting at a burrito place.

PAGE ONE

It was about three o’clock in the afternoon and I had yet to leave my house, nor did I have any particular plans to. Not only that but I was getting mighty hungry. So when my date from the previous week called me and then texted me that he was at a burrito place and wanted to bring over a burrito and his apparently new girlfriend Sarah, it seemed a little silly to say no, even though I hadn’t had a very good time on the date with him the first time and hadn’t really planned to go on any more with him.

But his girlfriend was coming, so I figured there was no way he could try to hook up with me. Besides, didn’t I always say I wanted to make some girlfriends in Portland? We went to the park with our burritos because we also wanted to drink the lovely dark six-pack they’d brought and my house was one of sobriety, as I may have mentioned previously.

We went to Brooklyn Park which, despite being two blocks from my house, I had never visited. We sat at a picnic table near the edge of the park — underneath the sky which was slowly fading to night. Sarah and I found that we had a few things in common: we were both from LA, we both liked photography, and our parents had encouraged us to follow similar paths in our lives.

Then Robin apparently felt he wasn’t getting enough attention so we changed the topic to one that could include him — astrology. After that we talked about various games we’d played as children — such as Thomas the Tank Engine, and about becoming artists in Portland. I got the feeling Robin wanted to remind me of the connection we had, and didn’t seem to like that Sarah and I seemed to be hitting it off without him.

When it became dark enough that we had trouble seeing, we returned to my house and, as it often seemed to, the subject of online dating came up. I hadn’t met any other girls who were familiar to the site, so I asked her some basic questions about her use of it, and she told me that she didn’t really need to message anyone since she got about five messages per day and Robin and I (but secretly) were surprised, both thinking that, being an attractive girl, she had to receive more.

It was hard to compare as I’d become accustomed to sending first messages to anyone who looked remotely appealing, but I couldn’t remember getting that many messages. In the time we’d been talking, Robin and Sarah had converged on the couch in our living room, while I pulled my black rolly chair over so I was seated in front of them.

I began to feel like a therapist as the topic of their relationship came up and I crossed my legs and pursed my lips. It seemed an unresolved quandary in both of their minds. They’d gone to a mountain together the night before and had worked out that they wanted a relationship after all, even though in the past Sarah hadn’t completely been on board for monogamy, and then Robin had done something to, well anyway, they were trying to figure out what label to have.

As they talked, they settled comfortably into lying next to each other, and I maintained my role, asking pertinent questions, but mostly just listening and making sure they each had a chance to speak. I made sure that they both got their voice heard, while staying as unbiased as possible, which was pretty unbiased since I couldn’t really figure any opinion to have about the situation.

I wasn’t clear on the exact particular reason why Sarah would choose Robin in the first place, and that may have been a missing link in trying to figure out what should go on in the future. At any rate, after they both had a chance to talk, they seemed to have resolved something, and I hurriedly got back to tinder so I could find a date to match their level of cuddliness.

I wondered if I should discreetly ask if he had just come from, or was planning on going to, a rave, but thought better of it and simply ushered him inside my house. I introduced him to everyone and, as you might imagine, awkwardness ensued. Though we’d already crossed the material boundary of the curtain which separated the living room from the kitchen, I asked him if he wanted me to make him tea, and tried to, thinking it was about time I become something more like a lady, except that I didn’t put the teapot on the right burner, and the longer we waited the longer absolutely nothing happened.

He got the impression, after I told him that I was a dancer because I had taken two modern dance classes in college, that I was a slightly different kind of dancer. I realized that I was standing a little too close for someone who I had just met, so I turned to take a few meaningful steps away from him, and, because my back was to him, he took advantage of the situation and slapped my butt just as my roommate walked in.
